claim: CDC25B phosphatase is required in mammals to finely tune neuronal production in the neural tube.
source: Here we show that the G2/M cell cycle regulator CDC25B phosphatase is required in mammals to finely tune neuronal production in the neural tube.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study, supported by the genetic loss-of-function experiments in mice described in the results.

claim: CDC25B activity favors fast nuclei departure from the apical surface in early G1 in chick neural progenitors.
source: We show that in chick neural progenitors, CDC25B activity favors fast nuclei departure from the apical surface in early G1, stimulates neurogenic divisions and promotes neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by time-lapse imaging data showing CDC25B increases Bs (basal) nuclear behavior in early G1.

claim: CDC25B stimulates neurogenic divisions in chick neural progenitors.
source: We show that in chick neural progenitors, CDC25B activity favors fast nuclei departure from the apical surface in early G1, stimulates neurogenic divisions and promotes neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by Sox2/Tis21 biomarker and Nucbow clonal analysis data.

claim: CDC25B promotes neuronal differentiation in chick neural progenitors.
source: We show that in chick neural progenitors, CDC25B activity favors fast nuclei departure from the apical surface in early G1, stimulates neurogenic divisions and promotes neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by HuC/D and Pax2 immunostaining data showing increased neuron production.

claim: Within a limited period of time, cell cycle length modifications cannot account for changes in the ratio of the mode of division.
source: We design a mathematical model showing that within a limited period of time, cell cycle length modifications cannot account for changes in the ratio of the mode of division.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by mathematical modeling showing that putative cell cycle times (17 to 172.7 hr) are incompatible with observed data.

claim: Part of CDC25B activity is independent of its action on the cell cycle.
source: Using a CDC25B point mutation that cannot interact with CDK, we show that part of CDC25B activity is independent of its action on the cell cycle.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments with CDC25B^ΔCDK mutant that affects neurogenesis without changing G2 phase length.

claim: The G1 phase is usually associated with the initiation of differentiation.
source: The G1 phase is usually associated with the initiation of differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The length of the G1 phase plays a major role in controlling cell fate decisions in neurogenesis, haematopoiesis and mammalian embryonic stem cells.
source: Notably, the length of the G1 phase has been shown to play a major role in controlling cell fate decisions in neurogenesis, haematopoiesis (Lange and Calegari, 2010) and mammalian embryonic stem cells (Coronado et al., 2013; Sela et al., 2012), including human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) (Pauklin and Vallier, 2013; Sela et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations to support the claim.

claim: During cortical neurogenesis, a lengthening of the G1 phase is associated with the transition from neural-stem-like apical progenitors to fate restricted basal progenitors.
source: During cortical neurogenesis, a lengthening of the G1 phase is associated with the transition from neural-stem-like apical progenitors (AP) to fate restricted basal progenitors (BP) (Arai et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Reducing G1 phase length leads to an increased progenitor pool and inhibition of neuronal differentiation.
source: Reducing G1 phase length leads to an increased progenitor pool and inhibition of neuronal differentiation, while lengthening G1 phase promotes the opposite effect (Calegari et al., 2005; Pilaz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Lengthening G1 phase promotes neuronal differentiation.
source: Reducing G1 phase length leads to an increased progenitor pool and inhibition of neuronal differentiation, while lengthening G1 phase promotes the opposite effect (Calegari et al., 2005; Pilaz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: G1 phase duration increases with neurogenesis in developing spinal cord.
source: In developing spinal cord, G1 phase duration increases with neurogenesis (Kicheva et al., 2014; Saade et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: In hESCs and in neurogenesis, the stem/progenitor cell uses Cyclin D to directly regulate the signaling pathways and the transcriptional program controlling cell fate choice.
source: Interestingly, in hESCs and in neurogenesis it has been shown that the stem/progenitor cell uses Cyclin D, which controls G1 phase progression, to directly regulate the signaling pathways and the transcriptional program controlling cell fate choice (Bienvenu et al., 2010; Lukaszewicz and Anderson, 2011; Pauklin et al., 2016; Pauklin and Vallier, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: A transient increase of epigenetic modifiers at developmental genes during G1 creates 'a window of opportunity' for cell fate decision in hESCs.
source: A transient increase of epigenetic modifiers at developmental genes during G1 has also been reported to create 'a window of opportunity' for cell fate decision in hESCs (Singh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Cell cycle genes involved in DNA replication and G2 phase progression maintain embryonic stem cell identity in hESCs.
source: Work on hESCs reveals that cell cycle genes involved in DNA replication and G2 phase progression maintain embryonic stem cell identity (Gonzales et al., 2015), leading the authors to propose that S and G2/M mechanisms control the inhibition of pluripotency upon differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: In the amphibian or fish retina, the conversion of slowly dividing stem cells into fast-cycling transient amplifying progenitors with shorter G1 and G2 phases propels them to exit the cell cycle and differentiate.
source: In the amphibian or fish retina, the conversion of slowly dividing stem cells into fast-cycling transient amplifying progenitors with shorter G1 and G2 phases, propels them to exit the cell cycle and differentiate (Agathocleous et al., 2007; Locker et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: A shortening of the S phase correlates with the transition from proliferative to differentiating (neurogenic) divisions in mouse cortical progenitors.
source: A shortening of the S phase correlates with the transition from proliferative to differentiating (neurogenic) divisions in mouse cortical progenitors (Arai et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Shorter S and G2 phases are associated with the neurogenic phase in the developing spinal cord.
source: In the developing spinal cord, shorter S and G2 phases are associated with the neurogenic phase (Cayuso and Martí, 2005; Kicheva et al., 2014; Le Dréau et al., 2014; Molina and Pituello, 2017; Peco et al., 2012; Saade et al., 2017, Saade et al., 2013; Wilcock et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations to support the claim.

claim: In developing neuroepithelia, cell cycle is synchronized with an oscillatory nuclear movement called Interkinetic Nuclear Migration (INM).
source: Notably, in developing neuroepithelia, cell cycle is synchronized with an oscillatory nuclear movement called Interkinetic Nuclear Migration (INM).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Nuclei of progenitor cells occupy specific positions according to cell cycle phase: nuclei migrate basally in the G1 phase, so that the S phase occurs on the basal side, and apically in the G2 phase, allowing mitosis to happen at the apical surface.
source: Nuclei of progenitor cells occupy specific positions according to cell cycle phase: nuclei migrate basally in the G1 phase, so that the S phase occurs on the basal side, and apically in the G2 phase, allowing mitosis to happen at the apical surface (Molina and Pituello, 2017; Norden et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: In mouse corticogenesis and in the chicken neural tube, nuclei migrate apically during G2 using the dynein/microtubule motor system.
source: In mouse corticogenesis and in the chicken neural tube, it was shown that nuclei migrate apically during G2 using the dynein/microtubule motor system (Baffet et al., 2015; Spear and Erickson, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: CDK1 triggers dynein recruitment to nuclear pores leading to apical nuclear movement during G2 phase.
source: It has been established that a key cell cycle regulator, the cyclin-dependent kinase 1 (CDK1), triggers dynein recruitment to nuclear pores leading to apical nuclear movement during G2 phase (Baffet et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: In the chicken spinal cord, zebrafish retina and rat neocortex, progenitor nuclei position along the apico-basal axis could lead to a differential exposure to proliferative or differentiative signals that could regulate progenitors cell fate.
source: In the chicken spinal cord, zebrafish retina and rat neocortex, it has been proposed that progenitor nuclei position along the apico-basal axis could lead to a differential exposure to proliferative or differentiative signals that could in turn regulate progenitors cell fate (Carabalona et al., 2016; Del Bene, 2011; Del Bene et al., 2008; Murciano et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: A link has been established between CDC25B phosphatase and neurogenesis.
source: A link has previously been established between a regulator of the G2/M transition, the CDC25B phosphatase and neurogenesis (Gruber et al., 2011; Peco et al., 2012; Ueno et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Three CDC25s A, B, C have been characterized in mammals.
source: Three CDC25s A, B, C have been characterized in mammals, and two, CDC25s A and B have been found in chick (Agius et al., 2015; Boutros et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Two CDC25s A and B have been found in chick.
source: Three CDC25s A, B, C have been characterized in mammals, and two, CDC25s A and B have been found in chick (Agius et al., 2015; Boutros et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The N-terminal region of CDC25B contains the regulatory domain.
source: The N-terminal region of CDC25B contains the regulatory domain, and the C-terminal region hosts the catalytic domain and the domain of interaction with known substrates, the CDKs (Sohn et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The C-terminal region of CDC25B hosts the catalytic domain and the domain of interaction with CDKs.
source: The N-terminal region of CDC25B contains the regulatory domain, and the C-terminal region hosts the catalytic domain and the domain of interaction with known substrates, the CDKs (Sohn et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: In Xenopus, CDC25B loss-of-function reduces the expression of neuronal differentiation markers.
source: In Xenopus, CDC25B loss-of-function reduces the expression of neuronal differentiation markers (Ueno et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: An upregulation of CDC25B activity associated with precocious neurogenesis has been observed in an animal model of microcephaly.
source: An upregulation of CDC25B activity associated with precocious neurogenesis has been observed in an animal model of microcephaly (Gruber et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: CDC25B expression correlates remarkably well with areas where neurogenesis occurs in the developing spinal cord.
source: Using the developing spinal cord as a paradigm, we previously reported that CDC25B expression correlates remarkably well with areas where neurogenesis occurs (Agius et al., 2015; Peco et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Reducing CDC25B expression in the chicken neural tube alters both cell cycle kinetics by increasing G2-phase length and neuron production.
source: We showed that reducing CDC25B expression in the chicken neural tube alters both cell cycle kinetics, by increasing G2-phase length, and neuron production (Agius et al., 2015; Peco et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Cdc25b is detected in the neural tube from E8.5 onward in the mouse embryo.
source: In the mouse embryo, Cdc25b is detected in the neural tube from E8.5 onward and remains strongly expressed in areas where neurogenesis occurs, as illustrated in the E11.5 neural tube (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cdc25b remains strongly expressed in areas where neurogenesis occurs in the mouse neural tube.
source: In the mouse embryo, Cdc25b is detected in the neural tube from E8.5 onward and remains strongly expressed in areas where neurogenesis occurs, as illustrated in the E11.5 neural tube (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The mitotic index displayed a slight and non-significant reduction in Cdc25b mutant embryos at E11.5.
source: Similarly, the fraction of mitotic cells assessed by quantifying the number of Phospho-Histone 3 (PH3) mitotic cells in the Pax7+ cells displayed a slight and non-significant reduction in the mitotic index of mutant embryos (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by PH3 immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: At E12.5, a significant reduction of 25.7% in the number of Pax2+ neurons is observed following Cdc25b deletion.
source: One day later, a clear and significant reduction of 25.7% and 28% in the number of Pax2+ and Tlx3+ neurons, respectively, is observed following Cdc25b deletion.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: At E12.5, a significant reduction of 28% in the number of Tlx3+ neurons is observed following Cdc25b deletion.
source: One day later, a clear and significant reduction of 25.7% and 28% in the number of Pax2+ and Tlx3+ neurons, respectively, is observed following Cdc25b deletion.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: Progenitor domain size measured at E11.5 and E12.5 using Pax7 or Sox2 immunohistochemistry shows non-significant differences between Cdc25b mutant and control embryos.
source: Progenitor domain size measured at E11.5 and E12.5 using Pax7 or Sox2 immunohistochemistry shows non-significant differences (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Analysis of dorsal progenitor nuclear density using DAPI shows a small and constant 7.5% reduction at E11.5 in mutant versus control embryos.
source: Analysis of dorsal progenitor nuclear density using DAPI shows a small and constant 7.5% and 7.3% reduction at E11.5 and E12.5, respectively, in mutant versus control embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that neuronal reduction is at least partly due to this small reduction in the progenitor population.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by DAPI staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Analysis of dorsal progenitor nuclear density using DAPI shows a small and constant 7.3% reduction at E12.5 in mutant versus control embryos.
source: Analysis of dorsal progenitor nuclear density using DAPI shows a small and constant 7.5% and 7.3% reduction at E11.5 and E12.5, respectively, in mutant versus control embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that neuronal reduction is at least partly due to this small reduction in the progenitor population.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by DAPI staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Quantification of active caspase three immunostaining at E12.5 does not reveal an increase in cell death in Cdc25b mutant embryos.
source: Quantification of active caspase three immunostaining (E12.5) does not reveal an increase in cell death, showing that the reduction in neuron number is not due to apoptosis (not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on immunostaining data.

claim: The ratio of dILA to dILB neurons is similar in control (0.68) and Cdc25b mutant embryos (0.71).
source: The ratio of dILA to dILB neurons is similar in control (0.68) and mutant embryos (0.71), confirming that Cdc25b does not impact specific neuronal cell type but rather has a generic effect on neuron production.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on quantification of Pax2 and Tlx3 neurons.

claim: Cdc25b does not impact specific neuronal cell type but rather has a generic effect on neuron production.
source: The ratio of dILA to dILB neurons is similar in control (0.68) and mutant embryos (0.71), confirming that Cdc25b does not impact specific neuronal cell type but rather has a generic effect on neuron production.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on the similar ratio of neuronal subtypes in control and mutant embryos.

claim: Efficient spinal neuron production requires CDC25B in mammalian embryos.
source: Together, these observations demonstrate that efficient spinal neuron production requires CDC25B in mammalian embryos and illustrate that this function is conserved among higher vertebrates.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the mouse genetic experiments.

claim: CDC25B function in neuron production is conserved among higher vertebrates.
source: Together, these observations demonstrate that efficient spinal neuron production requires CDC25B in mammalian embryos and illustrate that this function is conserved among higher vertebrates.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on observations in both mouse and chicken.

claim: The ccRE promoter is sufficient to drive lacZ reporter expression in the entire chicken neural tube after transfection by in ovo electroporation.
source: We verify that ccRE is sufficient to drive lacZ reporter expression in the entire chicken neural tube after transfection by in ovo electroporation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by lacZ staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Under the control of ccRE, the eGFP-CDC25B fusion protein is expressed in a subset of transfected cells.
source: Under the control of ccRE, the eGFP-CDC25B fusion protein is expressed in a subset of transfected cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The CDC25B gain-of-function does not induce apoptosis.
source: The gain-of-function does not induce apoptosis, as revealed by quantification of active caspase three immunostaining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by active caspase 3 immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: Ectopic expression of CDC25B shortens the G2 phase.
source: To ascertain that the phosphatase is functional, we analyze its impact on G2 phase duration. As expected, ectopic expression of the phosphatase shortens the G2 phase (Figure 2B, blue curve) without significantly modifying the mitotic index or the proliferation index (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by PLM assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CDC25B gain-of-function does not significantly modify the mitotic index.
source: As expected, ectopic expression of the phosphatase shortens the G2 phase (Figure 2B, blue curve) without significantly modifying the mitotic index or the proliferation index (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by PH3 immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: CDC25B gain-of-function does not significantly modify the proliferation index.
source: As expected, ectopic expression of the phosphatase shortens the G2 phase (Figure 2B, blue curve) without significantly modifying the mitotic index or the proliferation index (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by EdU labeling data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Quantitative analysis performed on the entire neural tube using NeuroD-reporter assay indicates that increasing CDC25B is sufficient to promote neuronal commitment.
source: Quantitative analysis performed on the entire neural tube using NeuroD-reporter assay indicates that increasing CDC25B is sufficient to promote neuronal commitment (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the ventral neural tube, CDC25B gain-of-function increases the percentage of HuC/D+ GFP+ cells from 61.6 ± 1.5% to 76.5 ± 0.9%.
source: In the ventral neural tube, CDC25B gain-of-function increases the percentage of HuC/D+ GFP+ cells from 61.6 ± 1.5% to 76.5 ± 0.9%.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by HuC/D immunostaining data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: In the dorsal spinal cord, CDC25B gain-of-function increases the proportion of HuC/D+ cells from 30.7 ± 1.34% to 41.8 ± 2.64%.
source: Similarly, in the dorsal spinal cord, the proportion increases from 30.7 ± 1.34% to 41.8 ± 2.64% with the CDC25B gain-of-function (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by HuC/D immunostaining data shown in Figure 2F,G.

claim: A significant increase in neurogenesis is observed using Pax2 immunostaining, from 11.4 ± 1% to 20 ± 1.8% following CDC25B gain-of-function.
source: A significant increase in neurogenesis is also observed using Pax2 immunostaining, from 11.4 ± 1% to 20 ± 1.8% (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Pax2 immunostaining data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: CDC25B gain-of-function reduces the proportion of cells expressing the progenitor marker Sox2.
source: Conversely, CDC25B gain-of-function reduces the proportion of cells expressing the progenitor marker Sox2 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Sox2 immunostaining data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: CDC25B is sufficient to stimulate neuron production.
source: Together, these results indicate that CDC25B is sufficient to stimulate neuron production.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the gain-of-function experiments.

claim: An increase in CDC25B activity has been shown to induce a shifted cleavage plane and precocious neurogenesis during corticogenesis in mouse.
source: An increase in CDC25B activity has been shown to induce a shifted cleavage plane and precocious neurogenesis during corticogenesis in mouse (Gruber et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: CDC25B gain-of-function does not induce a significant change in spindle orientation in spinal neural precursors.
source: We therefore tested the effect of CDC25B gain-of-function on spindle orientation in spinal neural precursors. We measured the angle of the mitotic spindle as previously described (Saadaoui et al., 2014), and we did not observe a significant change in spindle orientation (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by spindle angle measurements shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: CDC25B gain-of-function does not induce a significant modification of the spindle-size asymmetry (SSA) in chick spinal neural progenitors.
source: Another element implicated in asymmetric cell fate in neural progenitors is the spindle-size asymmetry (SSA), that is, the difference in size between the two sides of the spindle (Delaunay et al., 2014). Our CDC25B gain-of-function experiments did not induce a significant modification of the SSA in chick spinal neural progenitors (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by SSA measurements shown in Figure 3C–D.

claim: CDC25B activity does not affect the orientation or the size of the mitotic spindle.
source: In summary, our analyses did not reveal an effect of CDC25B activity on the orientation or the size of the mitotic spindle.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the spindle analysis experiments.

claim: Sox2+Tis21– cells expressing only Sox2::GFP correspond to PP divisions.
source: Briefly, the neural tube is electroporated with Sox2::GFP and Tis21::RFP reporters, and 24 hr later the number of neural progenitors expressing these markers is quantified at mitosis. Thus, Sox2+Tis21– cells expressing only Sox2::GFP correspond to PP divisions, Sox2–Tis21+ cells correspond to NN divisions, while cells co-expressing both biosensors Sox2+Tis21+ correspond mostly to asymmetric neurogenic divisions, PN (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the Sox2/Tis21 biomarker strategy.

claim: Sox2–Tis21+ cells correspond to NN divisions.
source: Briefly, the neural tube is electroporated with Sox2::GFP and Tis21::RFP reporters, and 24 hr later the number of neural progenitors expressing these markers is quantified at mitosis. Thus, Sox2+Tis21– cells expressing only Sox2::GFP correspond to PP divisions, Sox2–Tis21+ cells correspond to NN divisions, while cells co-expressing both biosensors Sox2+Tis21+ correspond mostly to asymmetric neurogenic divisions, PN (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the Sox2/Tis21 biomarker strategy.

claim: Cells co-expressing both Sox2 and Tis21 biosensors (Sox2+Tis21+) correspond mostly to asymmetric neurogenic divisions (PN).
source: Briefly, the neural tube is electroporated with Sox2::GFP and Tis21::RFP reporters, and 24 hr later the number of neural progenitors expressing these markers is quantified at mitosis. Thus, Sox2+Tis21– cells expressing only Sox2::GFP correspond to PP divisions, Sox2–Tis21+ cells correspond to NN divisions, while cells co-expressing both biosensors Sox2+Tis21+ correspond mostly to asymmetric neurogenic divisions, PN (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the Sox2/Tis21 biomarker strategy.

claim: There is no significant difference in the distribution of Sox2/Tis21 expressing cells in total neuroepithelial progenitors versus during mitosis in the dorsal spinal cord 24 hr post electroporation.
source: We do not detect a significant difference in the distribution of cells in total neuroepithelial progenitors (55.4 ± 6.2% Sox2+Tis21– cells, 29.3 ± 3.9% Sox2+Tis21+ cells and 15.2 ± 2.9% Sox2–Tis21+ cells) and during mitosis (57.9 ± 9.3% Sox2+Tis21– cells, 23.2 ± 8.5% Sox2+Tis21+ cells and 19 ± 7.3% Sox2–Tis21+ cells) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Recent data indicate that Sox2 mRNA expression can be sustained in some neurogenic progenitors.
source: Recent data indicate that Sox2 mRNA expression can be sustained in some neurogenic progenitors (Albert et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: A fraction of the Sox2+Tis21+ cells might correspond to NN rather than PN divisions.
source: A fraction of the Sox2+Tis21+ cells might therefore correspond to NN rather than PN divisions, suggesting that the use of these biomarkers is not sufficient to separate PN and NN divisions in our experimental conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference based on recent data about Sox2 expression.

claim: CDC25B RNAi electroporation leads to a consistent and strong downregulation in CDC25B transcripts located in the intermediate neural tube.
source: CDC25B RNAi electroporation leads to a consistent and strong downregulation in CDC25B transcripts located in the intermediate neural tube (Figure 4C, bracket).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CDC25B RNAi induces a massive increase in Sox2+Tis21– progeny from 13.4 ± 1.3% to 35.1 ± 1.8%.
source: When compared to the control scrambled RNAi, the CDC25B RNAi induces a massive increase in Sox2+Tis21– progeny (13.4 ± 1.3% to 35.1 ± 1.8%), and a decrease in Sox2+Tis21+ progeny (from 72.1 ± 1.85% to 56.2 ± 1.70% and to some extent, in Sox2–Tis21+ progeny (from 14.6 ± 1.43% to 8.74 ± 0.8%, Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Sox2/Tis21 biomarker data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CDC25B RNAi induces a decrease in Sox2+Tis21+ progeny from 72.1 ± 1.85% to 56.2 ± 1.70%.
source: When compared to the control scrambled RNAi, the CDC25B RNAi induces a massive increase in Sox2+Tis21– progeny (13.4 ± 1.3% to 35.1 ± 1.8%), and a decrease in Sox2+Tis21+ progeny (from 72.1 ± 1.85% to 56.2 ± 1.70% and to some extent, in Sox2–Tis21+ progeny (from 14.6 ± 1.43% to 8.74 ± 0.8%, Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Sox2/Tis21 biomarker data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CDC25B RNAi induces a decrease in Sox2–Tis21+ progeny from 14.6 ± 1.43% to 8.74 ± 0.8%.
source: When compared to the control scrambled RNAi, the CDC25B RNAi induces a massive increase in Sox2+Tis21– progeny (13.4 ± 1.3% to 35.1 ± 1.8%), and a decrease in Sox2+Tis21+ progeny (from 72.1 ± 1.85% to 56.2 ± 1.70% and to some extent, in Sox2–Tis21+ progeny (from 14.6 ± 1.43% to 8.74 ± 0.8%, Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Sox2/Tis21 biomarker data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CDC25B RNAi increases proliferative divisions from 13.4 ± 1.3% to 35.1 ± 1.8%.
source: Therefore CDC25B RNAi increases proliferative divisions from 13.4 ± 1.3% to 35.1 ± 1.8% and decreases neurogenic divisions from 86.6 ± 1.3% to 63.9 ± 1.8% (P-value < 0,0001).
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on Sox2/Tis21 biomarker data.

claim: CDC25B RNAi decreases neurogenic divisions from 86.6 ± 1.3% to 63.9 ± 1.8%.
source: Therefore CDC25B RNAi increases proliferative divisions from 13.4 ± 1.3% to 35.1 ± 1.8% and decreases neurogenic divisions from 86.6 ± 1.3% to 63.9 ± 1.8% (P-value < 0,0001).
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on Sox2/Tis21 biomarker data.

claim: CDC25B downregulation hinders neuron production by maintaining proliferative divisions and reducing neurogenic divisions.
source: This observation indicates that CDC25B downregulation hinders neuron production by maintaining proliferative divisions and reducing neurogenic divisions.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the RNAi experiments.

claim: CDC25B gain-of-function leads to a decrease in Sox2+Tis21– progeny from 46.1 ± 2.1% to 27.3 ± 1.8% in the entire neuroepithelium at 24 hr after electroporation.
source: Analyzing the distribution of the mode of division with the Tis21/Sox2 strategy in the entire neuroepithelium at 24 hr after electroporation, showed that CDC25B leads to a decrease in Sox2+Tis21– progeny (from 46.1 ± 2.1% to 27.3 ± 1.8%), an increase in Sox2+Tis21+ progeny (from 43.4 ± 1.9% to 50.9 ± 1.6%), and Sox2–Tis21+ progeny (from 10.5 ± 0.8% to 21.8 ± 1.5%, Figure 5A,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Sox2/Tis21 biomarker data shown in Figure 5A,D.

claim: CDC25B gain-of-function leads to an increase in Sox2+Tis21+ progeny from 43.4 ± 1.9% to 50.9 ± 1.6% in the entire neuroepithelium at 24 hr after electroporation.
